name: Nigeria
card_headline: Nigeria goes to a 16 January 2027 election after its most violent quarter on record, with inflation down to 14 percent and 200 US troops leaving
card_summary: ACLED data shows April to June 2026 was Nigeria's most violent quarter since 1997. Mass kidnappings continue across the north, and ISWAP has overrun army bases in Borno. About 200 US troops sent in February are leaving. The presidential vote is set for 16 January 2027, with Tinubu, Atiku and Obi running for three different parties. Inflation fell to 14.06 percent in October, but food prices are up 19 percent on the year. More than 17 million people in nine northern states face crisis-level hunger or worse.
card_local: Premium Times reports ACLED data showing Boko Haram events falling through 2026, while Daily Trust records that Borgu officials put the August mosque abductions near 60 against a community list of 547. [1][2]
card_international: Reuters and AFP report that suspected Boko Haram fighters killed 10 to 15 soldiers at a Borno base in October, and AP reports that the US is withdrawing 200 troops. [3][4][5]
card_scholar: ACLED's July overview records more than 900 deaths in Sokoto State in one year, and a CTC Sentinel study finds that JNIM now operates on Nigerian territory. [6][7]
context_md: Nigeria has about 240 million people. [8] President Bola Tinubu removed the fuel subsidy shortly after taking office in 2023 and loosened foreign-exchange rules. [9] The Boko Haram and ISWAP insurgency in the northeast is in its 17th year, has killed tens of thousands and has displaced around two million people, according to the UN as relayed by AFP. [4] In the northwest and north-central states, bandit gangs and kidnapping for ransom have grown, and analysts quoted by The New Humanitarian tie the violence to weak governance and rural poverty. [8] In November 2025 gunmen took schoolgirls in Kebbi and more than 300 students and teachers in Niger State, and on 25 December the US struck Islamic State targets in Sokoto State. [10][11] Freedom House rates Nigeria Partly Free, with 44 points out of 100. [12]

sections.title: The northeast: ACLED's Boko Haram count fell, but ISWAP keeps taking army bases
sections.body_md:
ACLED rates the second quarter of 2026 as the most violent in Nigeria since its records begin in 1997, with attacks on civilians by insurgents and bandits up 30 percent, according to Semafor's summary. [13] In the northeast the army has been losing bases. The ICIR counted at least eight attacks on military bases between January and 10 April, seven of them in Borno, the latest on 9 April at Benisheikh. It cites Daily Trust for a brigadier general and 17 soldiers killed there and notes that the Defence Headquarters gave no toll. [14]

The attacks continued into autumn. Suspected Boko Haram fighters overran an army base in Guzamala, Borno, on the night of 13 October, and two military sources told Reuters at least 10 soldiers died. [3] AFP later reported 15 soldiers and five militia members killed, the base burned and troops pulling back toward Monguno. [4] The army's own account of earlier fighting is more upbeat: in March it said attacks on forward bases at Mayanti, Gajigana and Gajiram were repelled and called them evidence of ISWAP's weakening capacity. [15] HumAngle describes a coordinated ISWAP assault on 12 and 13 May in which fighters took Marte, used drones at Rann and drove civilians toward the Cameroon border. [16]

Premium Times, using ACLED data, reports that events involving Boko Haram fell from close to 100 in the fourth quarter of 2025 to roughly 50 in the third quarter of 2026. ACLED's Ladd Serwat says the violence peaked in April and the group has intensified operations in Chad's Lac province and Cameroon's Far North. A June ceasefire with a Boko Haram faction led by Bakura Doro, said to have freed 360 abducted civilians, is denied by the military, and it did not cover ISWAP. [1]

lenses.local: Premium Times and the ICIR report the losses with figures from sources and ACLED, while Channels carries the army's statement that attacks were repelled. [1][14][15]
lenses.international: Reuters and AFP report the October base attacks with casualty figures from military sources. [3][4]
lenses.scholar: ACLED's Serwat attributes the fall in Boko Haram events to a shift of operations across the border into Chad and Cameroon, not to a ceasefire the army denies. [1]

sections.title: Kidnapping has moved from schools to mosques, and the counts are disputed
sections.body_md:
Amnesty International counted at least 1,100 people abducted across northern states between January and April 2026. Its list includes about 200 killed and 176 abducted at Woro in Kwara State on 3 February, more than 400 abducted at Ngoshe in Borno on 3 March, and at least 166 taken from a church at Kurmin Wali in Kaduna on 18 January. Amnesty says the figures likely understate the scale. [17] Authorities told AP that at least 162 people were killed at Woro and Nuku. [18]

On 21 August attackers hit four mosques in Borgu, Niger State, during Friday prayers. Affected communities published a list of 547 names. Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called reports of more than 500 abductees "social media hype" and put the figure at 63, and the Borgu council chairman said it was a little above 60. By 28 September the captives' whereabouts were unknown. [2] The chairman also said about 30 bodies had been buried, and Premium Times understood that the Dekara area had been under Ansaru's control. [19] A community head told Reuters at least 2,000 people fled into Benin. [20] This draft found no later report on the captives' release.

The business of ransom is growing. SBM Intelligence says ransom payments tripled to $5.8 million between July 2025 and 2026 and the number of kidnap victims rose 66 percent. [13] Police in Zamfara said more than 30 suspected bandits' bodies were found after a clash at Bukuyum on 28 October, a count they said was still unverified. [21] Sahara Reporters reported on 14 November that bandits killed two abducted victims in Niger State despite a ransom of N6 million. [22] ACLED records more than 900 deaths in Sokoto State over the year to June, and June 2026 was the state's deadliest month since 1997. [6]

The jihadist threat is spreading west. A CTC Sentinel study judges that JNIM now operates on Nigerian territory, though its size is unclear, and that most Lakurawa activity in Sokoto and Kebbi is Islamic State Sahel Province. [7] AFP reports videos that appear to show JNIM and ISSP fighting each other in Kebbi. [23]

lenses.local: Daily Trust and Premium Times document the gap between the community list of 547 and the official figure of about 60. [2][19]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, Reuters and AP carry the Borgu and Woro attacks and the presidential rescue order. [20][18]
lenses.scholar: The New Humanitarian reports analysts who see bandit violence as driven by economic gain and weak rural governance, and ACLED and CTC Sentinel track the jihadist spread. [8][6][7]

sections.title: US strikes and 200 US troops arrived in 2026, and the troops are now leaving
sections.body_md:
President Donald Trump designated Nigeria a Country of Particular Concern, according to CNN. [24] He said US forces struck Islamic State targets in Sokoto State on 25 December 2025, and a Defense Department official told AP that Nigeria approved the strikes, and Nigeria's foreign ministry described intelligence exchange and strategic coordination. [11] About 200 US troops arrived in February 2026. The Nigerian government says they helped with training and intelligence and joined an operation that killed a senior Islamic State leader. Nigeria confirmed on 1 September that they will leave, and military spokesman Samaila Uba said parts of the security partnership will continue. [5]

Semafor reports that Senator Ted Cruz has threatened sanctions and an aid freeze, and that Nigeria has spent at least $9 million on US lobbying. [13] CFR's Ebenezer Obadare writes that some northern clerics and leaders see the US partnership as having a "hidden agenda", and that this is one reason Tinubu is less popular in the north than three years ago. [25]

The religious framing is contested. CNN cites ACLED data for January 2020 to September 2025: more than 20,400 civilians killed, of which 317 deaths came from attacks targeting Christians and 417 from attacks targeting Muslims, with religion unrecorded for most victims. The same report quotes Pastor John Joseph Hayab of the Christian Association of Nigeria in the north, who agrees there are systematic killings of Christians. [24] The Nigerian government has said people of many faiths have suffered. [11]

lenses.international: AP reports the strike, the February deployment and the September withdrawal, and Semafor reports congressional pressure. [11][5][13]
lenses.scholar: CFR's Obadare ties northern opposition to the US partnership to Tinubu's weaker standing in the region. [25]
lenses.local: Local sourcing on the US role is thin in this draft; Nigerian reporting was read only through the military spokesman's quoted statement. [5]

sections.title: The January 2027 vote is the first under the Electoral Act 2026, with three main candidates in three parties
sections.body_md:
INEC set the presidential and National Assembly elections for 16 January 2027 and the governorship and state assembly elections for 6 February 2027. It moved them from 20 February and 6 March after the original dates drew backlash for clashing with Ramadan. INEC chairman Joash Amupitan said the new Electoral Act 2026 required a revised timetable. [26] Campaigning began on 19 August. [27]

INEC says the national register now stands at over 103 million voters, including 10,772,421 new registrations still subject to biometric verification. It began nationwide collection of permanent voter cards on 9 October and has acquired 57,000 new BVAS devices. [28][29]

The field has three main names. Tinubu is the APC's candidate and has led a party in power for nearly 12 years. [27] Atiku Abubakar won the ADC primary on 27 May with 1,846,379 votes against 540,117 for Chibuike Amaechi, and Peter Obi is the candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress. [30] Attempts to unite the opposition behind one candidate have failed. [9] Reuters cites SBM Intelligence's voter tracker, in which nearly 80 percent of Nigerians say the country is heading in the wrong direction, and Amnesty International's count of at least 10,217 killings by armed groups since Tinubu took office. [27] CFR's Obadare says Tinubu has weakened the PDP by encouraging governors to defect and warns of a drift toward a one-party state. [25] A former intelligence official told AFP that attacks often rise before elections. [23]

lenses.local: Daily Trust, Premium Times and Arise carry the INEC timetable, the voter register and the ADC primary result. [26][28][30]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera frame the vote as a test of Tinubu's economic reforms and his security record. [27][9]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House held a panel on 12 November on how the 2027 election could shape Nigeria's democratic path and regional stability, and CFR's Obadare calls the north Tinubu's weak point. [31][25]

sections.title: Journalists face Cybercrimes Act charges as the campaign runs
sections.body_md:
A federal court in Abuja on 10 November remanded Daniel Ojukwu, a reporter for the Foundation for Investigative Journalism, to Kuje Custodial Centre until a bail hearing on 1 December. He pleaded not guilty to 12 counts under the Cybercrimes Act and the Criminal Code. The charges come from four FIJ investigations of contracts in the office of a presidential aide on the Sustainable Development Goals. FIJ founder Fisayo Soyombo faces the same charges. [32] The Committee to Protect Journalists counts at least 29 journalists prosecuted under the cybercrimes law since 2015 and warns of the effect on press freedom before the elections. [32]

The pattern predates this case. CPJ reported in late 2025 that at least three journalists had been detained since August over alleged Cybercrime Act violations despite the law's amendment, with its Africa director saying authorities see the Act as a ready tool to harass the press. [33]

Freedom House scores Nigeria 44 out of 100 and Partly Free, citing criminal defamation laws and the harassment of journalists, and noting extrajudicial killings by security forces. [12] The Reporters Without Borders index ranks Nigeria 112th of 180 in 2026, up from 122nd, with a score of 48.11, as reported by Gatekeepers News. [34] On the separatist question, an Abuja court sentenced IPOB leader Nnamdi Kanu to life in prison on 20 November 2025, and analysts told Reuters the verdict could fuel sentiment in the southeast. [35]

lenses.local: The Cable and Gatekeepers News report CPJ's findings and the RSF ranking for Nigerian readers. [33][34]
lenses.international: Reuters reported the Kanu verdict and the court's reasoning. [35]
lenses.scholar: Freedom House and CPJ are the main structured sources on press and political freedom in this draft. [12][32]

sections.title: Inflation is down to 14 percent, but food costs 19 percent more and the naira is slipping
sections.body_md:
The National Bureau of Statistics put October headline inflation at 14.06 percent, down from 14.63 percent in September and 18.97 percent a year earlier. Food inflation was 19.13 percent, up from 16.30 percent in October 2025, and core inflation was 10.78 percent. Month on month, prices rose 0.43 percent. [36]

The World Bank forecast about 4.2 percent growth for 2026 in April and said fuel prices had risen more than 50 percent during the Iran war. [37] The IMF's April outlook put 2026 growth at 4.1 percent and 2027 at 4.3 percent. [38] Reuters reports that Tinubu ended the fuel subsidy and devalued the naira twice, which the government says restored stability, while critics point to the cost of living. It adds that GDP per capita reportedly fell 53 percent since 2015 and public debt rose more than twelvefold. [27]

The currency is weakening again. On 18 November the parallel-market rate reached N1,470 to the dollar, the weakest since 28 January, and the official rate closed at N1,363.23. External reserves were $43.64 billion on 14 November, down from $45.56 billion on 2 January. [39] CFR noted in April that supporters of the president cite reserves at a seven-year high of $46 billion. [25]

lenses.local: ThisDay and Techeconomy report the inflation print, the naira rate and the reserves. [36][39]
lenses.international: Reuters carries the World Bank forecast and the Reuters analysis of the subsidy and devaluation record. [37][27]
lenses.scholar: CFR's Obadare records the dispute between supporters who cite reserves and critics who cite deepening hardship. [25]

sections.title: Oil output is at its OPEC quota while the lithium boom has yet to pay its host communities
sections.body_md:
Nigeria produced an average of 1.687 million barrels a day of crude oil and condensate in October, according to the state upstream regulator NUPRC, quoted by the government's News Agency of Nigeria. Crude alone averaged 1.51 million barrels a day, 101 percent of the 1.5 million OPEC quota, the sixth month in a row at or above quota. Crude output fell 1.7 percent from September. [40] The regulator's own figures are the only source for this paragraph.

Lithium is the newer bet. Premium Times, in a series with The New Humanitarian, reports that Nigeria's lithium belt runs from Oyo in the southwest to Kano in the north and is estimated at more than $34 billion. Raw ore exports are banned, and Chinese investment in processing plants has reached $1.3 billion. At Kangimi in Kaduna State, a processing plant promised a clinic, roads and jobs, and three years later the clinic and roads are unbuilt, the village head says. Niger State's mines inspectorate has one vehicle and four staff. In September, 37 boys and young men died in Civil Defence Corps custody in Niger State after raids on mining sites. [41]

lenses.local: NAN, which is state-run, and Premium Times give opposite pictures: record quota compliance in oil and unbuilt promises in lithium. [40][41]
lenses.international: The World Bank has urged Nigeria to save windfalls from higher oil prices, as Reuters reported. [37]

sections.title: More than 17 million people in nine northern states face crisis-level hunger as aid shrinks
sections.body_md:
WFP's latest Cadre Harmonisé analysis finds more than 17 million people across nine conflict-affected northern states facing crisis, emergency or catastrophic hunger, nearly 2 million more than the previous assessment. In Borno, more than 3 million people are acutely food insecure and more than 10,000 have reached catastrophic levels. WFP says it can help only about 740,000 of the 6.2 million food-insecure people in the three northeastern states and needs $89 million for the next six months. An estimated 36.2 million people are food insecure nationwide. [42] In January WFP said it would reach only 72,000 people in February, against 1.3 million in the 2025 lean season, and that about 15,000 people in Borno were at risk of catastrophic hunger, the first such risk in nearly a decade. [43]

UNICEF's mid-year report says 8.4 million people need humanitarian assistance, including 5 million children, and that the northeast has 5.9 million people in severe need. About 1.4 million people are displaced in the northwest. Nigeria reported 26,848 cholera cases and 181 deaths by the end of June, with Borno the epicentre. UNICEF had received 28 percent of its $210.8 million appeal by mid-year. [44] The January humanitarian response plan counted 7.3 million people in need in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe. [45]

lenses.local: ThisDay carries WFP's warning on the scale of northern hunger and the funding shortfall. [42]
lenses.international: WFP, UNICEF and OCHA are the primary sources on need and funding. [43][44][45]
lenses.scholar: The New Humanitarian links kidnapping to higher food prices and lower food supply in the north. [8]

timeline.text: Gunmen abduct 25 schoolgirls from a girls' school in Maga, Kebbi State.
An Abuja court sentences separatist leader Nnamdi Kanu to life in prison on terrorism charges.
303 students and 12 teachers are abducted from St. Mary's school in Papiri, Niger State.
The US announces strikes on Islamic State targets in Sokoto State; Nigeria says it cooperated.
At least 166 worshippers are abducted from a church at Kurmin Wali, Kaduna State.
Gunmen attack Woro and Nuku in Kwara State; authorities later give at least 162 dead.
INEC moves the presidential election to 16 January 2027 and the governorship vote to 6 February 2027.
Insurgents attack the brigade headquarters at Benisheikh, Borno; Daily Trust reports a brigadier general among the dead.
Atiku Abubakar wins the ADC presidential primary; Peter Obi is the NDC candidate.
The second quarter ends as Nigeria's most violent in ACLED records since 1997.
Campaigning for the January election begins.
Gunmen attack four mosques in Borgu, Niger State, and abduct worshippers; counts range from about 60 to 547.
Nigeria confirms about 200 US troops sent in February will withdraw.
INEC says the voter register exceeds 103 million.
Suspected Boko Haram fighters overrun an army base in Guzamala, Borno; 10 to 15 soldiers are reported killed.
A federal court remands journalist Daniel Ojukwu on Cybercrimes Act charges; bail hearing set for 1 December.
NBS reports October inflation of 14.06 percent.
The naira reaches N1,470 to the dollar on the parallel market, its weakest since January.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and AFP file regularly on Nigeria and Al Jazeera, Semafor and CNN have covered the 2026 attacks, mostly when a mass kidnapping, a base attack or a US move breaks. [3][5][13] Nigerian outlets file daily on the same events, but the northwest bandit economy gets less wire attention than the northeast insurgency. [19][8]

severity.basis: ACLED rates April to June 2026 as Nigeria's most violent quarter since 1997, and it recorded about 4,518 deaths in jihadist incidents in 2025. [13][23]
More than 17 million people in nine northern states face crisis-level hunger or worse, and UNICEF counts 8.4 million people needing assistance with its appeal 28 percent funded. [42][44]
Freedom House scores Nigeria 44 out of 100, and CPJ reports a reporter held on Cybercrimes Act charges during the election campaign. [12][32]
Inflation is 14.06 percent with food at 19.13 percent, the naira is at its weakest parallel rate since January, and Reuters reports public debt up more than twelvefold since 2015. [36][39][27]
Violence reached a record in the second quarter of 2026 and aid has fallen, while inflation has eased from 18.97 percent a year earlier and growth is forecast near 4 percent. [13][42][36][38]

parts.basis: The US struck targets in Sokoto and deployed about 200 troops, and Chinese investment in lithium processing has reached $1.3 billion. [11][5][41]
Nigeria produced 1.687 million barrels a day of crude and condensate in October, and the World Bank forecasts growth near 4.2 percent in 2026. [40][37]

Militants move across the Niger, Nigeria and Benin borderlands, at least 2,000 people fled into Benin after the Borgu attacks, and Boko Haram operations have shifted into Chad and Cameroon. [23][20][1]
With about 240 million people, Nigeria is the home of an insurgency that has displaced around two million people. [8][4]
A US strike carried out with the host government's approval and a US troop deployment that is ending set a pattern for counterterrorism cooperation in West Africa. [11][5]

summary: Nigeria matters beyond its borders through its population, its oil, its role in the Sahel and Lake Chad borderlands and the US decision to treat it as a counterterrorism partner. [8][40][11] The score stays moderate because most of the violence is domestic and the US troop presence is ending. [5]
gi.up: A collapse of the January election or a jihadist group holding territory near the Benin or Niger borders.
gi.down: A credible, peaceful vote and a sustained fall in attacks on civilians.

reporters.bio: Wrote the 2 November 2026 Premium Times report on Nigeria's lithium boom, part of a series with The New Humanitarian, and the 19 November 2026 report on ACLED data on Boko Haram violence.
reporters.why: His recent work links ACLED conflict data with reporting on mining communities.

reporters.name: Elisha Bala-Gbogbo
reporters.bio: Co-wrote the 19 August 2026 Reuters analysis of Tinubu's re-election bid, and is credited with writing the 15 October 2026 Reuters report on the Borno base attack.
reporters.why: One of the main routes by which the election and the northeast insurgency reach international readers.
reporters.label: Reuters via The Star

reporters.name: Alexander Onukwue
reporters.bio: Wrote the August 2026 Semafor report on the mass abductions and ACLED's record quarter, which also covers the US troops, the army reshuffle and the state police proposal.
reporters.why: The report ties ACLED, SBM Intelligence and political reporting into one account of insecurity and the campaign.
reporters.label: Semafor

reporters.name: Nda Alhaji
reporters.bio: Wrote the 28 September 2026 Daily Trust report that set the community list of 547 names against the governor's figure of 63 after the Borgu mosque attacks.
reporters.why: Gives the clearest account of why the Borgu abduction numbers are disputed.
reporters.label: Daily Trust

reporters.name: Mustapha Usman
reporters.bio: Wrote the 10 April 2026 ICIR tally of attacks on military bases in the northeast since January.
reporters.why: The tally lists the officers killed and the places attacked in one place.
reporters.label: ICIR

reporters.name: Dyepkazah Shibayan
reporters.bio: Wrote the 1 September 2026 AP report confirming the withdrawal of about 200 US troops.
reporters.why: Reports the Nigerian military's account of the US deployment.
reporters.label: AP via ABC News

reporters.name: Ladd Serwat
reporters.bio: Provided the analysis for the ACLED data in the 19 November 2026 Premium Times report on Boko Haram violence.
reporters.why: Tracks how Boko Haram and ISWAP violence moves between Nigeria, Chad and Cameroon.
reporters.label: Premium Times

reporters.name: Ebenezer Obadare
reporters.role: Douglas Dillon Senior Fellow for Africa Studies, Council on Foreign Relations
reporters.bio: Wrote the 2 April 2026 CFR article 'Tinubu's Northern Trap', the first in a series ahead of the January 2027 election.
reporters.why: Explains the political cost to Tinubu of northern discontent and the US partnership.
reporters.label: Council on Foreign Relations

reporters.name: James Barnett
reporters.bio: Co-wrote the January 2026 CTC Sentinel study of jihadist expansion in Nigeria and wrote the October 2025 Hudson commentary on Lakurawa.
reporters.why: His work separates Lakurawa, JNIM, ISSP and Ansaru, which news reports often merge.
reporters.label: Hudson Institute

podcasts.guest: James Barnett (Hudson Institute), among four experts

factchecks.claim: Muslims killed more than 500,000 Christians in Nigeria in 2025.
factchecks.by: An unnamed speaker in a video shared on X
factchecks.evidence: Dubawa found no credible report supporting the figure and no official data on Christians targeted. It lists far lower counts: 11,968 total conflict deaths in Nigeria in 2025 (StatiSense), 3,490 Christian killings in Nigeria in Open Doors' October 2024 to September 2025 count, and 189,009 since 2009 from the NGO Intersociety, the highest figure it found. Dubawa's own verdict is insufficient evidence, and it notes that none of the figures are official.

sources.title: No proof Muslims killed 500,000 Christians in 2025

factchecks.claim: Violence in Nigeria is mainly aimed at Christians.
factchecks.by: US President Donald Trump and others
factchecks.evidence: CNN reports ACLED data for January 2020 to September 2025 showing more than 20,400 civilians killed, with 317 deaths in attacks targeting Christians and 417 in attacks targeting Muslims, and religion unrecorded for most victims. Attacks on Christian communities in 2025 are documented, and a northern church leader says the killings are systematic. The New Humanitarian reports analysts who locate the roots in weak governance and rural poverty.

factchecks.claim: About 63 people, not more than 500, were abducted from the Borgu mosques in August 2026.
factchecks.by: Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago, who called the larger figure social media hype
factchecks.evidence: Communities published a list of 547 names, families confirmed relatives in the kidnappers' video, and the Borgu council chairman gave a figure a little above 60. Daily Trust found the captives' whereabouts unknown on 28 September. No independent count has been located.

gaps: Punch could not be opened in this session, and The Cable and Channels are each cited once; local sourcing is thinner than the size of the Nigerian press warrants.
Sahara Reporters pages sat behind a bot check; the one item cited uses a headline only and is single-sourced.
HumAngle's article on the May 2026 ISWAP assault shows no publication date or author; the year is inferred.
No report was found on whether the Borgu mosque captives have been released, and no independent count of them exists.
The ACLED quarterly figures reach this page through Semafor, AFP and Premium Times; ACLED's own dataset was not queried.
Crisis Group's Nigeria pages were not reachable, so there is no Crisis Group citation; Chatham House appears only as an event page with no named speakers.
Amnesty International and Reporters Without Borders figures reach this page second hand through ThisDay, Reuters and Gatekeepers News.
Debt figures are Reuters' summary of critics' claims; no debt-to-GDP or debt-service data from the Debt Management Office or IMF was read.
Two of the three fact-checks rest on a CNN and a Dubawa report, not on a second independent check of ACLED's data.
The News Agency of Nigeria oil figures are the regulator's own and were not matched to OPEC's monthly report.
No documentary or photo essay was verified, so the media list is empty.
Rivers State politics, the southeast and Niger Delta, farmer-herder violence in Plateau and Benue, and ECOWAS relations with the Sahel juntas are not covered in this draft.

local_md:
Premium Times and the ICIR report the losses with figures from sources and ACLED, while Channels carries the army's statement that attacks were repelled. [1][14][15]

Daily Trust and Premium Times document the gap between the community list of 547 and the official figure of about 60. [2][19]

Local sourcing on the US role is thin in this draft; Nigerian reporting was read only through the military spokesman's quoted statement. [5]

Daily Trust, Premium Times and Arise carry the INEC timetable, the voter register and the ADC primary result. [26][28][30]

The Cable and Gatekeepers News report CPJ's findings and the RSF ranking for Nigerian readers. [33][34]

ThisDay and Techeconomy report the inflation print, the naira rate and the reserves. [36][39]

NAN, which is state-run, and Premium Times give opposite pictures: record quota compliance in oil and unbuilt promises in lithium. [40][41]

ThisDay carries WFP's warning on the scale of northern hunger and the funding shortfall. [42]
international_md:
Reuters and AFP report the October base attacks with casualty figures from military sources. [3][4]

Al Jazeera, Reuters and AP carry the Borgu and Woro attacks and the presidential rescue order. [20][18]

AP reports the strike, the February deployment and the September withdrawal, and Semafor reports congressional pressure. [11][5][13]

Reuters and Al Jazeera frame the vote as a test of Tinubu's economic reforms and his security record. [27][9]

Reuters reported the Kanu verdict and the court's reasoning. [35]

Reuters carries the World Bank forecast and the Reuters analysis of the subsidy and devaluation record. [37][27]

The World Bank has urged Nigeria to save windfalls from higher oil prices, as Reuters reported. [37]

WFP, UNICEF and OCHA are the primary sources on need and funding. [43][44][45]
scholar_md:
ACLED's Serwat attributes the fall in Boko Haram events to a shift of operations across the border into Chad and Cameroon, not to a ceasefire the army denies. [1]

The New Humanitarian reports analysts who see bandit violence as driven by economic gain and weak rural governance, and ACLED and CTC Sentinel track the jihadist spread. [8][6][7]

CFR's Obadare ties northern opposition to the US partnership to Tinubu's weaker standing in the region. [25]

Chatham House held a panel on 12 November on how the 2027 election could shape Nigeria's democratic path and regional stability, and CFR's Obadare calls the north Tinubu's weak point. [31][25]

Freedom House and CPJ are the main structured sources on press and political freedom in this draft. [12][32]

CFR's Obadare records the dispute between supporters who cite reserves and critics who cite deepening hardship. [25]

The New Humanitarian links kidnapping to higher food prices and lower food supply in the north. [8]
